newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt says Mideast needs action, not more promises.
newsitem.headline: Egypt says Mideast needs action, not more promises.

text.p: Egypt said on Wednesday that progress towards Middle East peace needed action, not just more promises from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
A senior Egyptian official, commenting on the outcome of the two-day Middle East summit in Washington, said the meeting did not seem to have bridged the gap between Israelis and the Palestinians.

"The differences remain the same and the whole exercise ended in more promises, more pledges. But promises and pledges by Netanyahu are not enough, what we need is deeds," said the official, who asked not to be named.
"If there are no moves, it will be a catastrophe," he added. "Throwing stones (by Palestinians) will look mild in comparison to what might happen."

Palestinian President Yasser Arafat went to Washington in the hope that U.S. President Bill Clinton might persuade Netanyahu to set a timetable for measures such as an Israeli withdrawal from the West Bank town of Hebron.
What he obtained was an Israeli commitment to keep talking.

Israeli cabinet secretary Danny Naveh said his country had "a great success". He added: "All the demands...we presented in the contacts and in the negotiations we've held night and day since coming here were accepted."
The Egyptian official said Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak had no need to justify his decision to stay away from the summit, which Egypt thought needed greater preparation.

Mubarak has also said he decided not to go when he realised that Netanyahu did not intend to make any gestures, even on the opening of a new entrance in a tunnel in Jerusalem which led to last week's violence between Israelis troops and Palestinians.
More than 70 people were killed in the clashes, the worst of their kind since Arafat went back to run the autonomous Palestinian areas in 1994.

"Such a summit should have had an agenda, some advance footwork by foreign ministers, details of points of disagreement and proposals for solving them. That is how summit are done," said the official.
"But I do share President Clinton's view that something had to be done. He did his maximum... He took a risk and we appreciate that," he added.

He noted that Clinton told the closing news conference he hoped that neither party would make changes in the status of Jerusalem -- an implicit criticism of Netanyahu's decision to reopen the tunnel near Moslem holy sites in the city.

But the official said that Palestinian patience was wearing thin. "The closures, the deteriorating economic situation -- the Palestinians are psychologically drained and the tunnel was the last straw that broke the camel's back," he added.
